question: For two independent Gaussian-subordinated long-memory series with one memory exponent below 1/2 and D_X+D_Y>1 (the mixed region), and for non-Gaussian marginals above the H_X+H_Y=3/2 line, what is the null limit of HSIC with a fixed bounded characteristic kernel?
setting: Kernel independence tests (HSIC) compare two series. With long memory their usual null theory can fail. The best existing theorem (Betken–Dehling, for distance covariance) covers two cases and openly leaves a third, 'mixed' case and the nonlinear high-memory case unproved.
proposed_contribution: A theorem, or a counterexample, for one fixed kernel and one specified pair of transforms, in the mixed region; with the kernel's leading Hermite coefficients written out.
importance: It decides whether the empirical sum-rule knot seen in the October 2026 simulation (H_X+H_Y≈1.5) has a theorem behind it for HSIC, not just for distance covariance.
remaining_uncertainty: Arcones 1994 and the newer U-process literature (e.g. 'Hermite ranks and U-statistics', HAL hal-01197638, abstract only, authors unverified) were not read in full; a general theorem may already imply the case.
feasibility: Pen-and-paper for one kernel and Gaussian inputs; a specialist proof check is needed. No data required.
fit: Directly continues TrackMB3 theory and the G1 proposal; uses the existing simulation as a check.

question: Can low-frequency (fixed number of cosine averages) inference in the style of Müller–Watson be applied to kernel feature maps to give an HSIC or MMD calibration that stays valid on both sides of the memory boundary without estimating H?
setting: G2 asks for a kernel test that works whatever the memory level. Econometrics already has a method that keeps coverage across many persistence types, but only for linear quantities. Whether it carries over to kernel tests is unknown.
proposed_contribution: A check of whether low-frequency averages of centred kernel features have a usable (Gaussian or tabulable) joint limit across the line; if yes, a calibrated H-free kernel test; if no, a stated obstruction.
importance: It is the only route found that has proven uniform coverage across fractional persistence, and it was missing from every earlier G2 review.
remaining_uncertainty: Worker inference, not in a source: above the line, low-frequency averages of rank-2 or cross features converge to non-Gaussian Hermite/Rosenblatt limits, so the Gaussian low-frequency framework may break exactly where it is needed.
feasibility: A derivation for one kernel, then a small simulation if the derivation is viable. Needs a separate author decision.
fit: Fits TrackMB3 and the author's econometrics strengths; reuses the simulation code base.

supporting_evidence.passage_or_section: Abstract and Section 'Coverage properties of restricted versions of the model' (Table 2 discussion): the general model 'controls coverage uniformly across these models'; I(0) sets have 'coverage of just 1%' under other persistence models
supporting_evidence.assessment: Uniform coverage over I(0), I(1), local-to-unity and fractional persistence is achievable for a linear second-moment (covariability) parameter using q≈12 low-frequency cosine averages. Linear only; relies on Gaussian low-frequency limits.

supporting_evidence.passage_or_section: Theorem 1 and discussion p.1335-1338: consistent LRV estimators 'necessarily lack robustness'; Theorem 1 is 'Rather than being a statement about the impossibility of valid inference'; Theorem 2(iv) fixed-b kernel estimators not robust to C2T(d)
supporting_evidence.assessment: Any long-run-variance estimator consistent in a benchmark model is fragile to small low-frequency contamination; inconsistent (low-frequency) estimators can be robust. Not an impossibility theorem for inference.

question: Does an |x|-type or squared transform of financial returns enjoy Hermite rank-2 protection under standard long-memory stochastic volatility models, with or without leverage?
setting: G3 hoped that symmetric transforms like |x| or x² keep a 'rank 2' property that delays the break to H=3/4. In the usual stochastic volatility model of returns, the memory sits in volatility, and the relevant rank is the rank of the volatility function.
proposed_contribution: None as a standalone gap. Use as a correction: in exponential-volatility models the relevant rank is 1, so the break for |r| or r² features is expected at H=1/2, not 3/4.
importance: Removes the finance premise of G3 in its model form; the narrowed G3 paper must not claim rank-2 protection for returns.
remaining_uncertainty: Model-level answer only. Whether real returns follow exp-LMSV, and the empirical rank, remain open (rank tests: Beran–Möhrle–Ghosh, abstract only in GAPLIT). The step 'E[|r| | X] = σ(X)E|Z|, so rank = rank of σ' is worker derivation for the no-leverage case.
fit: Corrects G3 and TrackMB3 finance wording.

supporting_evidence.passage_or_section: Section 5.1: 'for σ(x)=exp(x), τ*_p(s)=1 for all s'; Introduction: partial-sum theory 'entirely similar' with leverage but 'sample autocovariances may be very different in the presence of leverage'; Example 5.2: rank of K is 1 'except if E[Z_0 η_0]=0'
supporting_evidence.assessment: Kulik & Soulier (Adv. Appl. Probab. 44(4) 2012). In the standard LMSV model with exponential volatility, every power |Y|^p has Hermite rank 1 in the latent Gaussian; leverage changes ranks and rates of sample covariances.

contrary_evidence.assessment: Generic rank-instability mechanism already closed G3 as a standalone claim; consistent with, not contrary to, this finding.

question: Does the size of Hawkes likelihood-ratio Granger tests break at an H=3/4 memory line?
setting: Hawkes processes model event arrivals. Their 'memory' is the branching ratio and kernel tail, not a Gaussian Hurst index, so a 3/4 line has no theoretical basis there.
proposed_contribution: None as framed. Reframe the Hawkes arm by branching ratio, kernel tail and baseline misspecification.
importance: Keeps the cross-class paper from forcing Hawkes into a Hermite-rank frame.
remaining_uncertainty: Exploratory simulation (JOB-NEW-MEMORY-BOUNDARY-SIM-20261015 hawkes) shows size depends on ρ, kernel tail and baseline; the size-inflation mechanism under misspecification is not proved.

contrary_evidence.assessment: Kernel misspecification and regime shifts bias the branching ratio upward; already in TrackMB2 bibliography.
